title: InvestED, in order: a Rule #1 course
source: InvestED: The Rule #1 Podcast (Phil Town and Danielle Town), https://feeds.megaphone.fm/investedpodcast

modules.title: Orientation
modules.goal: Why Rule #1 investing, who's teaching, and how the course works.
modules.lesson:
1. **Retirement is a numbers problem you can't outsource to hope.** A typical plan is mostly the house plus a fund returning ~6%; after inflation it can run dry in about five years of drawing income, whereas the same savings at 15% changes the outcome ([029](episodes/029.md)).
2. **Compounding works both ways.** Inflation shrinks spending power and salaries lag it; debt compounds against you too ([030](episodes/030.md)).
3. **The best hedge is owning businesses with pricing power:** a moat lets a company raise prices with inflation.
4. **Two levers:** save more, and earn a higher return by learning to invest yourself.
5. Rule #1 (don't lose money) still frames everything; the retirement maths is *why* it matters.

modules.title: Understand the business
modules.goal: Circle of competence, the three circles, reading 10-Ks, and investing in line with your values.
modules.lesson:
Munger's four filters run in order, and **understanding** comes first: if you can't understand the business, stop.

1. **Find ideas without throwing darts.** Events (scary industry news), great investors' buys and the products you already use point you somewhere. They are tips, never decisions ([001](episodes/001.md), [011](episodes/011.md), [016](episodes/016.md)).
2. **Start inside your circles.** Overlap what you love, what you're good at and where you make and spend money. You know more than you think.
3. **Concentrate and dig your canyon.** An inch wide, a mile deep: few businesses studied hard (scuttlebutt plus filings) beat many studied lightly.
4. **Read the 10-K as a funnel** ([017](episodes/017.md)): Business, Risk Factors and MD&A first (several years, old to new), then peers' filings to see what's unusual. Check the company says plainly what makes it special ([018](episodes/018.md)).
5. **Check your values.** You own part of the company and vote with that money. Use values as a gate, not a premium.
6. **Respect the edge.** Losses happen at the boundary of your competence. When the 10-K stays murky or you feel tension, use the *too-hard* pile.
7. **Finish with the next question:** what is the moat, and do the numbers show it?

modules.title: Moats
modules.goal: The five moats (brand, secret, toll bridge, switching, price), how to spot a durable competitive advantage, and how to tell when it's eroding.
modules.lesson:
1. **A moat is an *intrinsic*, *durable* advantage** (Buffett's water around the castle): if you removed it the business would suffer, and rivals with the whole market cap still couldn't win ([003](episodes/003.md)).
2. **Five kinds (Phil's grouping, not exhaustive):** brand, secrets (patents), switching costs, toll bridge, and price, meaning *lowest cost*, not low price.
3. **A moat buys time.** IBM's lock-in let it pivot; a moat also lets a company survive weak managers.
4. **Moats need maintenance and can erode:** regulation removes one slowly; a brand is fragile to disappointment.
5. **Find the claim, then test it on the ground** ([018](episodes/018.md)): Item 1 of the 10-K should say what makes the company different. Then check stores, customers and competitors. If management can't say it, worry.
6. **The screen sees the result, not the cause:** high steady margins and returns (m4). The five types are the question to ask once a stock passes the numbers.

modules.title: Management
modules.goal: Owner-oriented, honest and capable leaders, and how to judge them from letters, calls and capital allocation.
modules.lesson:
1. **Integrity means integrated:** what you see is what you get. Talent is mainly **capital allocation**: keep cash and earn a high ROE on it, or give it back ([005](episodes/005.md)).
2. **Judge from documents:** shareholder letters (boilerplate, or candid about mistakes; dropped five-year plans), earnings calls (direct or evasive), biographies and share-count trends.
3. **Leaders, not only managers,** and stakeholders matter (Mackey's conscious capitalism), though your values decide how much weight.
4. **Use numbers as a scorecard** ([021](episodes/021.md)): debt, ROE and ROIC show what managers do with your money. A falling ROE after acquisitions signals overpaying.
5. **Refinement:** management matters *less* than the business. Prefer a moat so strong that, in Munger's words, an idiot could run it, because someday one will. A management mistake often creates the sale price.

modules.title: The numbers: Big Five and ROIC
modules.goal: ROIC, sales, EPS, equity (BVPS) and operating cash flow growth, plus debt, and what they reveal about a moat.
modules.lesson:
1. **ROE (profit ÷ equity) of 10%+ for ten years, not falling, with no debt** is the first proof of a moat ([004](episodes/004.md)). Ten years is long enough for competitors to attack.
2. **Later refinement: ROIC** (return on all invested capital, debt included) is the better number; with no debt, ROE and ROIC match, so Phil simplifies to *avoid debt* ([021](episodes/021.md), [022](episodes/022.md)).
3. **The big four growth rates:** equity (book value) per share, EPS, sales and operating cash flow per share. Look for each at about 10%+ a year and *moving together* ([019](episodes/019.md), [020](episodes/020.md)). Tangled lines (General Motors) mean too hard.
4. **Operating cash flow is the canary** that catches accounting fictions first; EPS is partly a "fiction" of accruals.
5. **The numbers are rear-view.** They show a moat existed; you still must understand why it will last ([023](episodes/023.md)).
6. **Score a real case** ([043](episodes/043.md)): Chipotle against seven numbers. Tech is mostly avoided because moats there erode fast ([022](episodes/022.md)).

modules.title: Valuation and margin of safety
modules.goal: Sticker Price, the MOS price, Payback Time, Ten Cap and the reasoning behind each.
modules.lesson:
1. **Price is what you pay, value is what you get;** a business isn't worth an infinite price ([006](episodes/006.md)). Value is cash that reaches the owner.
2. **Payback time:** price ÷ owner cash flow (P/E is a crude version). About eight years or less is a fair price; twenty is "forget it" ([008](episodes/008.md), [045](episodes/045.md)).
3. **Owner cash flow** = net earnings minus *maintenance* capex; growth capex is separate. **Cap rate** = first-year cash return on price, so $5 at 10% means paying about $50 ([050](episodes/050.md)).
4. **Sticker price, four inputs** ([009](episodes/009.md), [024](episodes/024.md), [046](episodes/046.md)): trailing EPS, ten-year growth rate, future P/E (lower of twice growth or historical high), then discount at the 15% MARR. Refinement: take growth from *all* the big four, not EPS alone.
5. **Buy at half the sticker price** (margin of safety) and sell near value. Aim for about 26% a year, a double in three years ([010](episodes/010.md)).
6. **Values veto, they don't discount** ([044](episodes/044.md)). Farms and buildings obey the same cap-rate logic ([032](episodes/032.md)).
7. **Don't call the market,** but stay rational: FOMO and endless waiting can both be greed ([041](episodes/041.md)).
8. **Estimates are back-window projections;** stress-test growth (store counts) and treat all figures as dated.

modules.title: Events and buying
modules.goal: Waiting for a business to go on sale, events, buying in tranches and building a watchlist.
modules.lesson:
1. **Mr. Market is moody; you may ignore him** and buy when fear puts a good business on sale ([007](episodes/007.md)). Volatility is not risk.
2. **A good event is temporary and fixable,** at a business you understand and priced clearly below value ([025](episodes/025.md)). A fall that isn't an event (Apple) is no sale.
3. **RULERS** ([012](episodes/012.md)): Radar, Understand, Love, Event, Reduce basis, Story. Buying as an owner, you *want* prices low, though the price must eventually return.
4. **Buy in tranches** as the price falls, and keep cash as an advantage.
5. **Whole-market gauges** only tell you how hard to hunt ([039](episodes/039.md)): wait in cash for "six-inch bars" inside your circle. Bargains come only after the first three filters.
6. **Invert the story:** write the bear case first. A drop after buying tests whether you understood.

modules.title: Psychology and practice
modules.goal: Fear, greed, patience, the tension signal, inversion and avoiding noise.
modules.lesson:
1. **Know what you don't know.** Even Buffett and Munger got a handful of ideas truly right; use a margin of safety for errors you can't foresee ([047](episodes/047.md)).
2. **Volatility is risk only if you may have to sell soon.** For a long-term owner of unchanged value, a fall is an opportunity ([048](episodes/048.md), [035](episodes/035.md)).
3. **Markets are emotional** (the efficient-market idea fails in the short run); govern your emotions and know the story so a drop isn't a surprise.
4. **Practise before money:** open a brokerage account, paper trade, size by conviction, use limit orders ([014](episodes/014.md)).
5. **Be mindful:** most people don't refuse to invest, they never look. A promise to yourself beats a goal ([027](episodes/027.md)).
6. **Stay a student** and widen the circle slowly.

modules.title: Portfolio and selling
modules.goal: Concentration, position sizing, when the story changes, and when to sell.
modules.lesson:
1. **Rank asset buckets by what they produce:** bonds are low risk and low return; gold and currency are hedges or too-hard bets (money is faith) ([036](episodes/036.md)); commodities are fungible, have no moat and come with leveraged futures ([037](episodes/037.md), [038](episodes/038.md)); annuities bet on your lifespan and inflation erodes them ([031](episodes/031.md)).
2. **Fees, taxes and misaligned incentives** destroy compounding in mutual funds ([015](episodes/015.md)); robo-advisors automate modern portfolio theory cheaply but carry crowding risk ([049](episodes/049.md)).
3. **Real estate follows the same rules;** a REIT adds liquidity, and the same four filters apply ([034](episodes/034.md)).
4. **Reduce basis** ([026](episodes/026.md)): dividends return capital, lowering your basis until the holding acts like a growing "equity bond". Reinvest the cash; buying beats selling.
5. **A dividend is only as safe as owner cash flow and low debt** ([028](episodes/028.md)); borrowed dividends are a warning. It is not a reason to buy.
6. **Wait.** When rates and markets are stretched, great companies exist but none are cheap.

modules.title: The masters
modules.goal: Buffett, Munger, Graham, Pabrai, Spier and others: their ideas and their records.
modules.lesson:
1. **Dhandho** ([013](episodes/013.md)): "don't lose money" means asymmetric bets, small loss if wrong, large gain if right. Measure risk as the time to earn your money back.
2. **Size by conviction;** cash is a position.
3. **Graham to Munger:** from hundreds of "cigar butts" to a few wonderful businesses.
4. **Speculation versus investing** ([042](episodes/042.md)): ask whether the return holds if nothing wonderful happens (the equity-bond test). Confidence alone isn't enough; narrow the world to what you understand.

modules.title: Case studies and interviews
modules.goal: Companies analysed on the show, and guests' stories and lessons.
modules.lesson:
1. **Real assets obey Rule #1** ([033](episodes/033.md)): understand them, find a durable edge (location), buy after a bust.
2. **Buffett's Nebraska farm and New York building** show a cash-flow return, a bust seller and a margin of safety working together.
3. **Specialists beat generalists;** break the overwhelming into small steps and use scuttlebutt.
4. **Cycles come to you,** so you can wait for the price.

glossary.definition: Don't lose money. Rule #2: don't forget Rule #1 (Buffett).
Meaning (understand it), Moat, Management, Margin of safety: Munger's four filters, applied in order.
The set of businesses you truly understand. Knowing where it ends matters more than how big it is.
Temporary bad news that puts a good business on sale.
Buying far enough below value (Rule #1: 50% of Sticker) that mistakes don't lose you money.
Making the best case against your idea, then rebutting it or walking away.
Buffett's thought experiment: only 20 purchases in a lifetime, so each must count.
Ideas you pass on because you can't understand them well enough.
A durable competitive advantage: brand, secrets, switching, toll bridge or low cost.
Return on equity: profit divided by shareholders' equity. Rule #1 wants 10%+ for ten years.
Return on invested capital: profit on all capital, debt included. Better than ROE once debt is in play.
Equity (book value), EPS, sales and operating cash flow per share, each ideally growing 10%+ together.
Phil's estimate of value today: grow EPS ten years, apply a future P/E, discount at 15%.
Minimum acceptable rate of return: 15% a year in Rule #1.
Years of cash flow needed to earn back the price paid. About eight or fewer is a fair price.
Net earnings minus maintenance capex: the cash an owner could take out.
First-year cash return on purchase price; the price test for real estate and cash-flow businesses.
Graham's moody business partner who quotes a price daily; you may ignore him.
The theory that price already reflects all information. Rule #1 relies on it failing in the short run.
Modern portfolio theory calls price movement risk; Rule #1 says a falling price on unchanged value lowers risk.
Lower the money at risk in a holding by taking cash back, such as dividends.
A business whose cash payout to you grows over time, like a bond whose coupon keeps rising.
Radar, Understand, Love, Event, Reduce basis, Story: Phil's checklist.
A narrow area you study deeply: an inch wide and a mile deep.
Gathering information from customers, employees, suppliers and competitors.
Gujarati for endeavours that create wealth: low-risk, high-uncertainty bets (Pabrai).
Real estate investment trust: a listed company owning property that passes income to shareholders.
A contract paying income for life; essentially a bet on your lifespan that inflation erodes.
Cash generated by running the business; catches accounting fictions first.
Ability to raise prices without losing customers; the inflation hedge.
Valuing a holding at today's quoted price rather than its value.
